knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```{r setup}
library(httr2)
```

Almost every API requires you to identify yourself with a credential: an API key, a token, or a password.
These secrets need to be available to your code, but they must not leak to anyone else.
This article describes how secrets leak, then shows you how httr2's secrets system keeps them safe: give httr2 a *recipe* for a secret instead of its value, and httr2 will resolve it only when the request is performed and redact it everywhere else.

```{r, include = FALSE}
# In real life you'd set these in your .Renviron, not with Sys.setenv()
Sys.setenv(EXAMPLE_TOKEN = "token123", YOURPACKAGE_KEY = secret_make_key())
```

## Where secrets leak

There are three main ways that credentials accidentally escape:

1.  **Committed code.**
    If you paste a key into a script, it will end up in your git history, and if you type it into the console, it ends up in your `.Rhistory`.

2.  **Console output.**
    httr2 requests print their headers (via `print()`, `req_dry_run()`, and `req_verbose()`), so a credential embedded in a header can end up in log files, rendered documents, and bug reports.
    httr2 redacts secrets wherever it displays them, so you'll see `<REDACTED>` instead of the value.

3.  **Saved objects.**
    Responses, errors, and `last_request()` all carry the full request, so credentials can reach disk whenever such an object is saved: explicitly with `saveRDS()`, or implicitly with knitr caching, targets, or saving `.RData`.
    This is the sneakiest leak, and it's the main motivation for the approach described in the next section.

## Defer, don't embed

The core idea is simple: don't give httr2 the value of a secret; give it a recipe for obtaining the value.
httr2 resolves the recipe only when the request is performed, and redacts it everywhere it displays the request:

```{r}
req <- request("https://example.com") |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(secret_envvar("EXAMPLE_TOKEN"))
req
```

The header shows `<redacted (env: EXAMPLE_TOKEN)>`, so you can see *how* the secret will be obtained without seeing its value.
And because the request only stores the recipe, saving it to disk can't leak the value either.

## Four kinds of secret

### `secret_envvar()`

`secret_envvar()` records the name of an environment variable and reads its value at perform time.
This is the recommended default: environment variables are easy to set without typing anything into the console, and every deployment platform supports them.
Store the value in your `.Renviron` for local work (open it with `usethis::edit_r_environ()`), in your CI system's secret store, or in the environment variable settings for Posit Connect or Workbench:

```{r}
request("https://example.com") |>
  req_headers(`X-API-Key` = secret_envvar("EXAMPLE_TOKEN"))
```

Because the value is read each time the request is performed, rotating the env var takes effect on the next perform, with no need to rebuild the request.

### `secret_value()`

Use `secret_value()` for a value you already have in a variable: a function argument, a token returned by a login call, or a password you just prompted for.
The value is held in a weak reference so that it is never written to disk:

```{r}
request("https://example.com") |>
  req_headers(`X-API-Key` = secret_value("token123"))
```

The flip side is that the value doesn't survive `saveRDS()` and `readRDS()`, or a trip to a parallel worker: a reloaded `secret_value()` is silently dropped from headers, and errors when revealed from a body.
If a request needs to survive saving, use one of the other kinds of secret.

### Functions

Any zero-argument function that returns a string can be used as a secret, which makes it easy to plug in other credential stores, like keyring, askpass, or a secret manager's CLI:

```{r}
#| eval: false
request("https://example.com") |>
  req_headers(`X-API-Key` = \() keyring::key_get("example"))
```

### `obfuscated()`

`obfuscated()` is for mildly secret values that must be embedded in package code, like OAuth client secrets.
`obfuscate()` scrambles a string so that you can include it in your public source code without making it trivially readable:

```{r}
obfuscate("my-super-secret-token")
```

You then copy and paste the `obfuscated()` call into your code.
This is obfuscation, not encryption: the secret can't be revealed by inspecting your source code or scraped by automated tools, but a skilled R programmer could uncover it with some effort.

## Where secrets work

You can use secrets in the most common places that credentials are needed:

| Place                                        | Secrets supported |
|----------------------------------------------|:-----------------:|
| `req_headers()`                              |        ✅         |
| `req_auth_basic()` password                  |        ✅         |
| `req_auth_bearer_token()`                    |        ✅         |
| `req_auth_aws_v4()` credentials              |        ✅         |
| `req_body_json()`, `req_body_form()`, `req_body_multipart()` | ✅ |
| `oauth_client()` secret                      |        ✅         |
| `req_url_query()`                            |     Not yet       |
| `req_cookies_set()`                          |     Not supported |
| `req_proxy()` credentials                    |     Not supported |
| `req_options()`                              |     Not supported |

## Seeing what's sent

Redaction is the default everywhere httr2 displays a request, but sometimes you need to check the actual values.
`req_dry_run()` and `httr2_translate()` both have escape hatches:

```{r}
req <- request("https://example.com") |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(secret_envvar("EXAMPLE_TOKEN"))

httr2_translate(req)
httr2_translate(req, secrets = "reveal")
```

For bodies, use `req_get_body()` with `secrets = "reveal"` (or `"redact"`/`"remove"`).

It's also worth knowing exactly what happens when a request is saved, because saving happens in surprising places (knitr caching, targets, parallel workers).
Env var and obfuscated recipes are saved as recipes, so they still work when the request is reloaded or sent to a `mirai`/`callr`/targets worker.
`secret_value()`s and redacted plain headers are deliberately dropped, so a reloaded request has to re-add them:

```{r}
req <- request("https://example.com/get") |>
  req_headers(
    `X-Env` = secret_envvar("EXAMPLE_TOKEN"),
    `X-Value` = secret_value("token123")
  )

path <- tempfile()
saveRDS(req, path)

# X-Env still resolves; X-Value is gone
str(req_dry_run(readRDS(path), quiet = TRUE)$headers)
```

A function secret is saved along with whatever it captures, so it's up to you to make sure it only captures non-sensitive values.

## Encrypting secrets in a package

If you're developing a package that wraps an API, you'll need your own credentials for testing, and those credentials need to be available to you and your CI, but not to package users.
For this, httr2 provides a separate set of tools to encrypt secrets so that you can include them in your public source code without worrying that others can read them.
(This is likely overkill if you have one secret that only needs to be shared in a couple of places: you can just put it in your `.Renviron` and access it with `Sys.getenv()`.)

### Basics

There are three basic steps:

1.  Create an **encryption key** with `secret_make_key()`; this key scrambles and descrambles secrets using symmetric cryptography:

    ```{r}
    key <- secret_make_key()
    key
    ```

    (Note that `secret_make_key()` uses a cryptographically secure random number generator provided by OpenSSL; it is not affected by R's RNG settings, and there's no way to make it reproducible.)

2.  Scramble your secrets with `secret_encrypt()` and store the resulting text directly in the source code of your package:

    ```{r}
    secret_scrambled <- secret_encrypt("secret I need to work with an API", key)
    secret_scrambled
    ```

3.  When needed, descramble the secret using `secret_decrypt()`:

    ```{r}
    secret_decrypt(secret_scrambled, key)
    ```

### Package keys

You can create any number of encryption keys, but we highly recommend creating one key per package, which we'll call the **package** key.
httr2 is built around the notion that this key should live in an environment variable.
So the first step is to make your package key available on your local development machine by adding a line to your user-level `.Renviron` (which you can easily open with `usethis::edit_r_environ()`):

```
YOURPACKAGE_KEY=key_you_generated_with_secret_make_key
```

Now (after you restart R), you can take advantage of a special `secret_encrypt()` and `secret_decrypt()` feature: the `key` argument can be the name of an environment variable, instead of the encryption key itself.
In fact, this is the most natural usage:

```{r}
secret_scrambled <- secret_encrypt("secret I need to work with an API", "YOURPACKAGE_KEY")
secret_scrambled
secret_decrypt(secret_scrambled, "YOURPACKAGE_KEY")
```

You'll also need to make the key available in your GitHub Actions (both check and pkgdown) so your automated tests can use it.
This requires two steps:

1.  Add the key to your [repository secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/encrypted-secrets).

2.  Share the key with the workflows that need it by adding a line to the appropriate workflow:

    ``` yaml
        env:
          YOURPACKAGE_KEY: ${{ secrets.YOURPACKAGE_KEY }}
    ```

    You can see how httr2 does it in [its GitHub workflow](https://github.com/r-lib/httr2/blob/master/.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml){.uri}.

Other continuous integration platforms will offer similar ways to make a key available as a secure environment variable.

### Using an encrypted secret in a request

A scrambled secret is safe to capture in a function, which makes `\() secret_decrypt(enc, "YOURPACKAGE_KEY")` a convenient way to use an encrypted testing credential in a request:

```{r}
enc <- secret_encrypt("my-testing-api-key", "YOURPACKAGE_KEY")

req <- request("https://example.com") |>
  req_headers(`X-API-Key` = \() secret_decrypt(enc, "YOURPACKAGE_KEY"))
req
```

The request stores the ciphertext, not the plaintext, and only decrypts it when the request is performed.

### When the package key isn't available

There are a few important cases where your code won't have access to your package key: on CRAN, on the personal machines of external contributors, and in automated checks on their PRs.
So if you want to share your package on CRAN or make it easy for others to contribute, you need to make sure that your examples, vignettes, and tests all work without error:

-   In vignettes, you can run `knitr::opts_chunk(eval = secret_has_key("YOURPACKAGE_KEY"))` so that chunks are only evaluated if your key is available.

-   In examples, you can surround code blocks that require your key with `if (httr2::secret_has_key("YOURPACKAGE_KEY")) {}`.

-   You don't need to do anything in tests because when `secret_decrypt()` is run by testthat, it will automatically `skip()` the test if the key isn't available.

## Testing

Secrets are designed to be invisible to your tests when they need to be:

-   If the env var named by a `secret_envvar()` isn't set, the test is skipped (via `testthat::skip()`), just like with `secret_decrypt()`.
    Outside of testthat, a missing env var is an error.

-   Mocks see the unresolved request: `req_perform(mock =)` and `with_mocked_responses()` inspect the request before secrets are resolved, so your mock can match on the request without the secret ever being read, and secret functions won't be called at all if the request is never performed.

## Secrets in packages

Putting this all together, if you're writing a package that wraps an API, you no longer need a hand-written `get_api_key()` helper.
Instead, give your wrapper function an `api_key` argument that defaults to a `secret_envvar()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
my_api_request <- function(endpoint, api_key = secret_envvar("MYAPI_KEY")) {
  request("https://api.example.com") |>
    req_url_path_append(endpoint) |>
    req_auth_bearer_token(api_key)
}
```

This pattern has several nice properties:

-   The env var is read each time a request is performed, so if the user changes it mid-session, the next request picks up the new value.

-   The key only needs to exist when a request is actually performed, so users can load your package and read documentation without setting it.
    (And in tests, a missing key skips rather than errors.)

-   Users who can't or don't want to use an env var can supply the key directly: `my_api_request("endpoint", api_key = secret_value("their-key"))`.
    A plain string also works, but you should nudge users away from it because it will end up in their `.Rhistory`.

-   Whatever the user supplies, the key is redacted from console output and kept out of saved responses as much as possible.

For your own testing credentials, use the encryption approach described above: encrypt your key with a package key stored in the `MYAPI_KEY`-style env var on your machine and in your CI secret store, and let missing credentials skip your tests automatically.
